components.text: Explain why the epistemic priority of experience supplies positive support for a theistic conclusion.
Address whether acknowledging consciousness prevents a naturalistic position that rejects eliminativism.
Epistemic priority of experience does not by itself establish that naturalism is false or that God explains consciousness.
Provide a positive reason to treat consciousness as irreducible rather than merely pointing to an unresolved scientific gap.
Show whether the proposed account yet yields distinctive explanatory support for God.
Consciousness is directly known and irreducible, so the issue is ontological and not merely a temporary scientific gap.
Explain what idealism contributes beyond the shared distinction between reality and imagination.
Supply a warranted bridge from irreducible consciousness or idealism to God.
Deny that epistemic priority alone resolves the reality-versus-imagination distinction.
Calling experience fundamental does not remove the shared need to distinguish reality from imagination or establish God.
Explain why God is not a superfluous addition to a mind-first or idealist ontology.
Provide a criterion distinguishing the proposed conscious ground from imagination or fantasy.
Supply positive explanatory gain rather than relying only on the limits of material explanation.
God is not an optional addition if a conscious or mind-like basis is necessary for any universe to exist.
Theism purports to add a fundamental conscious ground rather than merely appeal to an unexplained scientific gap.
Provide positive evidence or explanatory gain for mentality beyond brain activity rather than an unresolved possibility.
Explain why possible brain-independent mentality warrants introducing God.
A mind-first position must distinguish a real brain-independent mentality from a merely coherent imagined possibility.
A coherent possibility of brain-independent mentality does not itself show explanatory gain for God.
Provide evidence that personal mentality can persist independently of the present brain.
Distinguish a real future embodiment from a merely imaginable metaphysical scenario.
A proposed alternative embodiment still requires grounds distinguishing real personal persistence from an imagined scenario.
Alternative embodiment does not establish that God provides additional explanation.
Show why logical possibility or a coherent re-embodiment model makes belief in survival reasonable.
Provide evidence that near-death reports disclose mentality independent of brain activity.
Distinguish conceivability of dualism from evidential support for its actuality.
Logical possibility of dualism or reembodiment does not establish that belief in survival is reasonable.
Near-death inquiry must provide actual evidence for mentality independently surviving brain function.
Explain what conception of God is being introduced and what explanatory role it is intended to perform.
Show that God provides more than an external intervention appended to an unexplained universe.
Supply evidence that the proposed conscious ground exists rather than merely redescribing it.
God is introduced as the universe's own conscious, purposive, intelligent ground rather than an external interfering agent.
The proposed explanatory gain is an immanent conscious ground, not an interventionist addition to nature.
The conception of God does not provide the requested evidence for survival or near-death claims.
Show why transformative religious experience identifies God as its best explanation rather than an evolved imaginative response.
Establish that experiences independently support the specific conscious and purposive divine ground proposed.
Distinguish religious interpretation from the ordinary reality-versus-imagination problem.
Transformative religious experience may arise through evolved psychology and imagination rather than disclose God.
Variable religious experiences do not uniquely support the proposed conscious purposive divine ground.
Answer the claim that incompatible cultural forms undermine religious experience as evidence.
Answer the evolutionary explanation of persistent religious cognition.
Address the contrast with scientific repeatability and independent verification.
Divergent interpretations may overlay a common experiential core, so diversity need not defeat religious experience.
Evolutionary persistence need not debunk experience because selection often favors cognition that tracks reality.
Address whether evolved cognition can be truth-conducive and therefore resist evolutionary debunking.
Explain whether pragmatic usefulness can substitute for the claimed transcendent explanation.
A naturalistic moral framework does not answer whether religious experiences share a truth-conducive transcendent core.
The assertion that God is unnecessary for morality bears against one proposed role for a divine ground.
Explain why an evolved or pragmatic moral framework is inadequate when obligation conflicts with inclination.
Establish that a divine ground is specifically required rather than some other objective normative basis.
Answer the broader evolutionary explanation by showing a distinct failure in moral commitment.
An evolved or socially inherited morality may lack a theoretical basis strong enough to sustain costly obligation.
Show why meaningful choice or commitment requires escape from causal determination rather than action through one's reasons and character.
Answer the suggestion that genuine willing must extend beyond the causal operations of a physical brain.
Address whether personal agency requires persistence in another embodiment.
Meaningful willing need not occur outside causal determination because compatibilism makes freedom consistent with causation.
The move does not answer the separate claim that moral commitment needs an objective theoretical ground.
Show why shared phenomena uniquely support a conscious, purposive, intelligent divine ground over competing paradigms.
Establish that irreducible consciousness selects a theistic rather than another metaphysical interpretation.
Show that experiential commonality resolves rather than illustrates interpretive underdetermination.
Show that moral experience uniquely requires a divine ground.
Show that freedom or willing uniquely requires a God-centered interpretation.
Shared phenomena permit radically different coherent interpretations and therefore do not uniquely establish a divine ground.
Agreement that consciousness is mysterious does not uniquely determine Ward's ontology.
Shared experiential language can coexist with incompatible paradigmatic interpretations.
Shared moral experience does not alone determine a divine grounding account.
